citation: Flondell M, Rosén B, Andersson G, Björkman A. Carpal tunnel syndrome treated with guided brain plasticity: a randomised, controlled study. J Plast Surg Hand Surg 2017;51(3):159-164 (advance online 12 Jul 2016).
text_quality: ok (born-digital publisher PDF of the advance-online article, same DOI, title and authors as the 2017 issue; PDF page 1 is the publisher cover page and the article is on PDF pages 2-7; Figure 1, the CONSORT flow chart on PDF page 4, is an image and was read from the rendered page; Table 2 read in the layout view)
design: Prospective randomised, placebo-cream-controlled, parallel-group trial at one centre. Computer-generated randomisation list (Excel). The two therapists who did all direct assessments and administered the questionnaires, and the neurophysiologist, were blind to treatment; the researcher who randomised the patients and applied and removed the cream (MF) was not. The placebo cream was visually and cosmetically identical to the active cream; the paper does not state that patients were blinded and does not use the words double-blind. Planned sample 66 (90% power, 5% significance) to detect a difference of 0.8 (SD 1.0) in the BCTQ symptom severity scale. Analysis: t-tests of change from baseline between groups, and within groups with a Bonferroni-corrected threshold (p < 0.004).
population: 70 adults with clinically and electroneurography-verified carpal tunnel syndrome (symptoms for more than 3 months, clinical signs, fractionated sensory conduction velocity across the wrist of 40 m/s or less), referred to the Department of Hand Surgery, Skåne University Hospital, Malmö, 2009-2015; 16 men and 54 women, mean age 49 (SD 9). Excluded: rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, neurological disease, multiple systemic disease, vibration-induced neuropathy, complete conduction block, allergy to local anaesthetics. Patients were not selected or characterised by pain, and baseline pain is not reported. Most had normal hand sensibility at baseline (abnormal touch threshold in 9 of 70, two-point discrimination over 5 mm in 2 of 70); median conduction velocity across the carpal tunnel 31 m/s.
n: Randomised 70: EMLA 34, placebo 36 (305 assessed, 235 excluded). Analysed 68: EMLA 32 (the CONSORT chart records 2 who withdrew after the first treatment because of local discomfort), placebo 36. Surgery status at 12 months reported for 32 and 36.
setting: Department of Hand Surgery, Skåne University Hospital, Malmö, Sweden; first application at the hospital (patients observed for adverse events), later applications self-administered at home with sensory re-education.
intervention: Lidocaine-prilocaine eutectic cream (EMLA, AstraZeneca) [dose figure omitted], applied to the volar forearm on the side of the carpal tunnel syndrome (the paper's area: 'from the wrist and 15 cm proximal'; in bilateral cases the more symptomatic side), not to the hand or the median-nerve territory, combined in both arms with sensory re-education and advice on using the hand in daily activities. The aim was to deafferent the forearm skin so that more cortical neurons serve the hand (guided plasticity), not analgesia of the symptomatic area. Schedule, as the study did it: three applications in week 1, two a week in weeks 2-6 and one a week in weeks 7-8 (15 applications over 8 weeks), each left on for 90 minutes and then washed off; the first at the hospital, the rest at home.
comparator: Placebo cream, visually and cosmetically identical, applied to the same forearm area on the same schedule, with the same sensory re-education.
route: Topical, cutaneous, volar forearm (proximal to and outside the painful or numb median-nerve territory of the hand).
duration: 8-week treatment programme; assessments at baseline, 90 minutes after the first application (sensory tests only) and at 8 weeks; surgery (carpal tunnel release) recorded at 12 months; all participants were offered surgical decompression after the 8 weeks.
outcomes: Primary: Boston Carpal Tunnel Questionnaire symptom severity scale (SSS; Levine 1993; mean of 11 items scored 1 best to 5 worst, labelled '0–5' in Table 2) at 8 weeks. The published SSS has 5 pain items (night pain severity, night waking from pain, daytime pain, daytime pain frequency, duration of daytime pain episodes) and 6 items on numbness, tingling, night numbness or tingling, weakness and difficulty grasping small objects; the paper reports only the total score, with no item or pain/numbness subscale breakdown. Secondary: QuickDASH (activity limitation), satisfaction with treatment on a 0-100 VAS, touch threshold (Semmes-Weinstein monofilaments, index finger), two-point discrimination (index finger), sensory electroneurography, carpal tunnel release by 12 months. No pain measure of any kind (no pain VAS or NRS); the word pain appears once, in the introduction.

key_results.quote: Seventy patients with clinical and electroneurography-verified CTS were randomised to sensory training combined with either an anaesthetic cream (EMLAV) (n ¼ 34) or a placebo cream (n ¼ 36) on the volar part of the forearm.
The primary outcome was the Boston carpal tunnel questionnaire (BCTQ) symptom severity scale after 8 weeks.
EMLAV or placebo was applied to the volar aspect of the forearm, in an area from the wrist and 15 cm proximal on the same side as the CTS.
After 90 minutes, the cream was washed off.
An 8-week treatment programme ([dose figure omitted]) was used.
Two therapists – who were blind regarding the treatment and who were experienced in assessment of nerve function – carried out all the direct assessments and administered the PROMs.

There was no significant difference in the BCTQ symptom severity scale between the EMLAV group and the placebo group when comparing baseline and 8 weeks (p ¼ 0.78, mean difference ¼ 0.05 units, 95% CI ¼ 0.3–0.4).
The BCTQ symptom severity scale had improved significantly in the EMLAV group after 8 weeks (p ¼ 0.001).

However, in absolute numbers the improvement was 0.5 units in the BCTQ symptom severity scale that goes from 1–5, where 0.8 units is considered a clinically important change [15]. Thus, the improvement may be of limited clinical importance (Table 2).

A reduction of symptoms in the BCTQ symptom severity scale was also seen in the placebo group after 8 weeks, but this difference was not significant. This might be the reason for the lack of a group difference at 8 weeks.
Furthermore, there were no significant differences between the EMLAV group and the placebo group when comparing changes in outcome between baseline and 8 weeks, regarding QuickDASH, SWM, and 2PD.

Mean patient satisfaction after 8 weeks, estimated on a visual analogue scale, was 53 (SD ¼ 28) in the EMLAV group and 40 (SD ¼ 28) in the placebo group. The difference between groups was not statistically significant, however.
ENeG did not show any significant differences after 8 weeks, either within groups or between the two groups (Table 2).
In the present study, patients treated with EMLAV showed an improvement in sensibility after 90 minutes, although this was not significant after correction for multiple comparisons (p ¼ 0.02).
However, repeated treatment with EMLAV did not consolidate the initial improvement in sensibility.

Despite this, 1 year after inclusion in the study, 15 of the 32 patients in the EMLAV group (47%) and 22 of the 36 patients in the placebo group (61%) had chosen a surgical intervention for their CTS.
No treatment-related adverse events were observed in any of the groups.
An 8-week treatment protocol with cutaneous forearm anaesthesia to guide brain plasticity gave no significant subjective or objective improvements in hand function compared to placebo.

author_limitations.quote: This study had some shortcomings. Although CTS is relatively common, it was difficult to recruit patients.

The sensory assessments used here could not capture the relief of symptoms experienced by the patients in the EMLAV group. This could indicate that the sensitivity of the test instruments was too low.

This skewed distribution of the data with a ceiling effect, with very few study participants below cut-off for normality in both touch thresholds and discriminative touch at … baseline (Table 2), means that the changes after 8 weeks of treatment could only be very small.
Only nine of the 70 participants had abnormal touch threshold (SWM above filament no. 2.83) at baseline, and only two had 2PD over 5 mm at baseline.

Further studies are needed to identify which patients with CTS may benefit from this treatment. Also, the optimal treatment protocol in terms of timing and duration of treatment would have to be decided on.

Note: the results say no treatment-related adverse events were observed, while the CONSORT chart records 2 EMLA patients who withdrew after the first treatment because of local discomfort.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Rosén B, Björkman A, Lundborg G. Improved sensory relearning after nerve repair induced by selective temporary anaesthesia - a new concept in hand rehabilitation. J Hand Surg Br 2006;31(2):126-32 (ref 10; the paper prints the volume as 13)
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Randomised double-blind trial: lidocaine-prilocaine cream or placebo cream applied repeatedly to the flexor forearm of the injured arm over a 2-week period after median or ulnar nerve repair (EMLA n=7, placebo n=6), with sensory re-education; sensory outcomes, no pain endpoint. Bears on D066 (repeated non-daily application in an established neuropathy) and on any claim counting placebo-controlled randomised trials of this cream.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Lundborg G, Björkman A, Rosén B. Enhanced sensory relearning after nerve repair by using repeated forearm anaesthesia: aspects on time dynamics of treatment. Acta Neurochir Suppl 2007;100:121-6 (ref 17)
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Prospective randomised double-blind study of repeated cutaneous forearm anaesthesia with sensory re-education after median or ulnar nerve repair; tactile gnosis better than placebo up to 4 weeks after the last session, no difference at 8-11 months; appears to report the same programme as Rosén 2006 with longer follow-up. Source of the schedule this trial used. Bears on D066 and D067 (placebo-controlled, no pain endpoint).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Rosén B, Björkman A, Lundborg G. Improving hand sensibility in vibration induced neuropathy: a case-series. J Occup Med Toxicol 2011;6:13 (ref 12; the paper prints '2011;13:3104948', i.e. article number and PMCID run together)

Bears on D066 (long repeated non-daily application in an established neuropathy).
